title: Typography
summary: Typography rules control how text looks and how easy it is to read.

subtopics.title: Main property
subtopics.explanation: A font family chooses the design of letters. A fallback list gives the browser another choice if the first font is unavailable, like carrying a backup pen. For example, `font-family: Arial, sans-serif` ends with a generic family. Prefer readable body fonts and reserve decorative faces for short headings.

subtopics.title: What it changes
subtopics.explanation: Font size controls how large text appears. Units such as `rem` scale from the document’s root text size, which can respect user preferences. It is like choosing the size of print on a sign. Set a clear type scale for headings and body copy, then verify it at zoom.

subtopics.title: Another useful choice
subtopics.explanation: Line height is the vertical space reserved for each line. If it is too small, lines feel crowded; if too large, paragraphs become harder to follow. It is like spacing lines in a notebook. A unitless value such as `1.5` scales with font size and often suits body text.

subtopics.title: Common behavior
subtopics.explanation: Font weight controls how thick letter strokes appear. Values such as 400 and 700 commonly mean regular and bold when the font provides those weights. It is like using a thicker marker for a heading. Do not use weight alone to show an error; include clear wording or another cue.

subtopics.title: Good practice
subtopics.explanation: Long lines make readers move their eyes too far between one line and the next. Limit paragraph width, often with a measure such as `65ch`. It is like keeping a page column narrow enough to scan. Check headings and real text at phone and desktop widths.

foundations.overview: Typography is the way text looks and reads on a page. CSS lets you choose letter shapes, size, spacing, weight, and line length. Think of typography like choosing a readable voice for a sign: the words matter, but their shape helps people understand them. Start with a system font stack, comfortable text size, and enough space between lines. Then check the page on a phone and with zoom enabled.
foundations.whyItMatters: Typography shapes how quickly people can scan and understand content. A coherent scale, comfortable measure, and resilient fallbacks help across screens and zoom.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser matches font-family against installed and loaded fonts, downloads web fonts, then shapes and lays out glyphs during layout. font-display decides what shows while a web font loads (e.g. swap shows fallback text immediately, avoiding invisible text).
foundations.realWorldUsage: Setting a base font and line-height on body, scaling headings with rem, loading a brand font via woff2, styling links by toggling text-decoration, and uppercasing eyebrow labels with text-transform are everyday tasks.
foundations.businessImpact: Typography is brand: consistent type builds recognition and trust, and faster-loading fonts (woff2, font-display: swap, system stacks) reduce bounce by avoiding blank or flashing text.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Centralizing type choices in variables/tokens (sizes, weights, line-heights) keeps a codebase consistent and easy to restyle, and unitless line-height plus rem sizing avoid a class of nesting and accessibility bugs.
foundations.performanceImpact: Web fonts add network weight; using woff2, subsetting characters, preloading the critical font, and font-display: swap minimize layout shift and blocked rendering. The system font stack costs nothing to download.

commonMisconceptions.myth: px is fine for font-size everywhere.
commonMisconceptions.reality: rem respects the user's browser font-size setting, so it's more accessible; px ignores it. Prefer rem for type.

commonMisconceptions.myth: line-height should always have a unit like 24px.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A unitless line-height (e.g. 1.5) scales with font-size and inherits cleanly; fixed units can break when font-size changes.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A larger font size alone guarantees readable text.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Line length, line height, contrast, language support, and hierarchy also affect readability.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Using bold is enough to mark an error.
commonMisconceptions.reality: State changes need clear text or another cue; weight alone may be missed.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A font size alone determines readability.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Line length, line height, contrast, language support, and hierarchy also affect reading comfort.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Bold styling is a complete way to signal importance.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Use meaningful text or another cue so the message survives visual differences and assistive use.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A generic sans-serif fallback renders the same on every device.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The browser chooses a system font, so its metrics and appearance vary across platforms.

visualExplorer.title: How a font stack resolves
visualExplorer.caption: Walk through how the browser picks the first available font in a stack and how the other type properties shape the result.

steps.title: Read the font-family list
steps.description: The browser reads fonts left to right: "Inter", "Helvetica Neue", Arial, sans-serif.

steps.title: Pick the first available
steps.description: It uses the first font that's installed or loaded; if Inter is missing it tries Helvetica Neue, then Arial.

steps.title: Fall back to the generic family
steps.description: If none match, it uses the generic keyword (sans-serif) so text still renders sensibly.

steps.title: Apply size and weight
steps.description: font-size (rem) and font-weight set how big and bold the glyphs render.

steps.title: Apply spacing
steps.description: line-height sets vertical rhythm; letter-spacing and word-spacing tune horizontal gaps.

steps.title: Apply presentation
steps.description: text-align, text-decoration, and text-transform finalize alignment, underlines, and casing.
